Our findings suggest that CDMs can serve not just as image generators but also as compact, interpretable teachers that can drive robust representation learning.

papers.title: Attention Sinks in Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of attention sinks in Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) and how do they differ from those in autoregressive models?
papers.core_contribution: DLMs exhibit dynamic attention sinks that shift during generation and are robust to masking, unlike autoregressive models, revealing fundamental differences in attention allocation.
papers.conclusion: DLMs have dynamic attention sinks and are robust to their removal, indicating flexible attention mechanisms that differ from autoregressive models.
papers.key_findings:
DLMs exhibit attention sinks, but they are dynamic and shift positions during the denoising process.
DLMs are robust to masking of attention sinks, with only minor performance degradation, unlike autoregressive models which are highly sensitive.
Different DLM architectures show distinct sink patterns: LLaDA-8B sinks are semantically based, Dream-7B sinks are positional, and MMaDA-8B sinks are static.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to instruct models and does not include base versions.
The study does not explore how modifications to the training procedure might influence sink behavior.
future_direction: Mechanistic analysis of what information is stored in sinks corresponding to future positions, e.g., using Logit Lens.
Exploring whether sinks could be exploited for acceleration or compression.
Detailed explanation of the observed sink phenomena, which would require an interpretability-focused study.
papers.abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to traditional Autoregressive Models (ARMs). DLMs employ transformer encoders with bidirectional attention, enabling parallel token generation while maintaining competitive performance. Although their efficiency and effectiveness have been extensively studied, the internal mechanisms that govern DLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis of DLM attention patterns, focusing on the attention sinking phenomenon, an effect previously observed in various transformer-based architectures. Our findings reveal that DLMs also exhibit attention sinks, but with distinct characteristics. First, unlike in ARMs, the sink positions in DLMs tend to shift throughout the generation process, displaying a dynamic behaviour. Second, while ARMs are highly sensitive to the removal of attention sinks, DLMs remain robust: masking sinks leads to only a minor degradation in performance. These results provide new insights into the inner workings of diffusion-based language models and highlight fundamental differences in how they allocate and utilize attention compared to autoregressive models.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: SAeUron: Interpretable Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we remove unwanted concepts from text-to-image diffusion models in an interpretable way using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAeUron, an interpretable concept unlearning method for diffusion models that uses sparse autoencoders to identify and ablate concept-specific features, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: SAeUron provides an effective, interpretable, and robust approach to concept unlearning in diffusion models by leveraging sparse autoencoders to localize and ablate concept-specific features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on diffusion model activations across multiple denoising timesteps learn sparse, interpretable features corresponding to specific concepts.
SAeUron outperforms existing methods on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for style and object unlearning and effectively removes nudity.
SAeUron is robust to adversarial attacks and can unlearn multiple concepts simultaneously with a single SAE.
The features selected for unlearning are interpretable, allowing for transparency and analysis of the unlearning process.
SAeUron does not require fine-tuning the base model, preserving its overall performance.
papers.limitation:
When two classes are highly similar (e.g., cats and dogs), unlearning one may negatively impact the generation quality of the other due to overlapping features.
Struggles to remove abstract concepts (e.g., hate, harassment) because SAE features correspond to visual elements rather than abstract notions.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models, while powerful, can inadvertently generate harmful or undesirable content, raising significant ethical and safety concerns. Recent machine unlearning approaches offer potential solutions but often lack transparency, making it difficult to understand the changes they introduce to the base model. In this work, we introduce SAeUron, a novel method leveraging features learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to remove unwanted concepts in text-to-image diffusion models. First, we demonstrate that SAEs, trained in an unsupervised manner on activations from multiple denoising timesteps of the diffusion model, capture sparse and interpretable features corresponding to specific concepts. Building on this, we propose a feature selection method that enables precise interventions on model activations to block targeted content while preserving overall performance. Our evaluation shows that SAeUron outperforms existing approaches on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for concepts and style unlearning, and effectively eliminates nudity when evaluated with I2P. Moreover, we show that with a single SAE, we can remove multiple concepts simultaneously and that in contrast to other methods, SAeUron mitigates the possibility of generating unwanted content under adversarial attack. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/cywinski/SAeUron.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: $\textit{Revelio}$: Interpreting and leveraging semantic information in diffusion models
papers.research_question: What flavors of visual information are captured in different layers and timesteps of a diffusion model? How do they interact and complement each other? What inductive biases are captured in convolution-based vs transformer-based diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Revelio, a method using k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE) to uncover monosemantic interpretable features in diffusion models, and demonstrates the effectiveness of diffusion features for transfer learning via a lightweight classifier (Diff-C).
papers.key_findings:
Representation granularity varies non-linearly with model depth, with different layers capturing varying levels of visual semantics.
Representation granularity and generalizability vary with diffusion architectures, pre-training data, and design choices like latent vs pixel space.
k-sparse autoencoders help isolate monosemantic visual properties across model states, aiding interpretation.
Diffusion features are effective for discriminative tasks and visual reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight classifier.
Different diffusion timesteps capture different information granularities, with earlier timesteps better for fine-grained tasks.
future_direction: Deeper investigation into why additional noise at certain timesteps (e.g., t=200) helps feature generalizability.
Further research to understand why SD 1.5 performs better than SD 2.1 across timesteps, as noted in prior zero-shot classification work.
papers.abstract: We study $\textit{how}$ rich visual semantic information is represented within various layers and denoising timesteps of different diffusion architectures. We uncover monosemantic interpretable features by leveraging k-sparse autoencoders (k-SAE). We substantiate our mechanistic interpretations via transfer learning using light-weight classifiers on off-the-shelf diffusion models' features. On $4$ datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of diffusion features for representation learning. We provide an in-depth analysis of how different diffusion architectures, pre-training datasets, and language model conditioning impacts visual representation granularity, inductive biases, and transfer learning capabilities. Our work is a critical step towards deepening interpretability of black-box diffusion models. Code and visualizations available at: https://github.com/revelio-diffusion/revelio

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models memorize training data? The paper investigates the underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models, focusing on why and how it occurs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that memorization in diffusion models is driven by overestimation of training samples during early denoising, caused by classifier-free guidance, which collapses latent diversity and locks denoising trajectories onto memorized images.
papers.conclusion: Memorization arises from overestimation of memorized data in early denoising, and recognizing this regime could lead to safer, less replicative generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone; with classifier-free guidance, training loss is larger in early denoising under memorization.
Memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, steering denoising toward paired samples.
Classifier-free guidance leads to overestimation of the training image, which grows linearly with the guidance scale.
Overestimation collapses latent diversity and causes denoising trajectories to converge quickly to the memorized image.
Deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule (in terms of contributions of x and x_T) correlate strongly with memorization severity.
papers.abstract: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can memorize training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has sought to characterize, detect, and mitigate memorization, the fundamental question of why and how it occurs remains unresolved. In this paper, we revisit the diffusion and denoising process and analyze latent space dynamics to address the question: "How do diffusion models memorize?" We show that memorization is driven by the overestimation of training samples during early denoising, which reduces diversity, collapses denoising trajectories, and accelerates convergence toward the memorized image. Specifically: (i) memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone, as training loss is larger under memorization due to classifier-free guidance amplifying predictions and inducing overestimation; (ii) memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, forcing latent trajectories to converge and steering denoising toward their paired samples; and (iii) a decomposition of intermediate latents reveals how initial randomness is quickly suppressed and replaced by memorized content, with deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule correlating almost perfectly with memorization severity. Together, these results identify early overestimation as the central underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models.

papers.title: Concept Sliders: LoRA Adaptors for Precise Control in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we enable precise, interpretable control over attributes in image generations from diffusion models using low-rank parameter directions (concept sliders) derived from text or image pairs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Sliders, a method to create low-rank LoRA adaptors for diffusion models that enable precise, continuous, and composable control over image attributes with minimal interference.
papers.conclusion: Concept Sliders provide a simple and scalable paradigm for interpretable control of diffusion models, enabling continuous, single-pass adjustments and complex multi-concept manipulation beyond text-driven methods.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Sliders allow precise control over image attributes using text prompts or image pairs, with minimal entanglement.
Sliders are composable, enabling complex multi-attribute control by overlaying multiple low-rank directions.
The method can transfer latent directions from StyleGAN to diffusion models for nuanced visual control.
Concept Sliders can fix common distortions in generated images, such as improving hand realism and overall image quality.
A disentanglement objective and low-rank constraint are key to achieving targeted edits with reduced interference.
papers.limitation:
Some residual interference between edits remains, indicating a need for more careful selection of preservation directions.
The SDEdit inference technique helps preserve structure but can reduce edit intensity compared to full inference-time application.
papers.abstract: We present a method to create interpretable concept sliders that enable precise control over attributes in image generations from diffusion models. Our approach identifies a low-rank parameter direction corresponding to one concept while minimizing interference with other attributes. A slider is created using a small set of prompts or sample images; thus slider directions can be created for either textual or visual concepts. Concept Sliders are plug-and-play: they can be composed efficiently and continuously modulated, enabling precise control over image generation. In quantitative experiments comparing to previous editing techniques, our sliders exhibit stronger targeted edits with lower interference. We showcase sliders for weather, age, styles, and expressions, as well as slider compositions. We show how sliders can transfer latents from StyleGAN for intuitive editing of visual concepts for which textual description is difficult. We also find that our method can help address persistent quality issues in Stable Diffusion XL including repair of object deformations and fixing distorted hands. Our code, data, and trained sliders are available at https://sliders.baulab.info/

papers.title: Patronus: Interpretable Diffusion Models with Prototypes
papers.research_question: How can the diffusion generation process be interpreted and understood? Specifically, what visual patterns emerge during generation, where and when they appear, and to what extent they can be controlled.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Patronus, an interpretable diffusion model that integrates a prototypical network to encode semantics in visual patches, revealing what visual patterns are modeled and where and when they emerge during denoising.
papers.conclusion: Patronus offers valuable insights into interpretable diffusion models by bridging diffusion and prototypical networks, enabling interpretation of the generation process and supporting semantic manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Patronus captures semantically meaningful features within images and achieves competitive generative performance.
Patronus can diagnose shortcut learning by detecting unwanted correlations via prototype similarity scores.
Prototypes emerge at different times during the generation process, with lower spatial frequency attributes appearing earlier and higher spatial frequency attributes later.
Patronus enables semantic manipulation of images by adjusting prototype activation vectors.
The model learns prototypes without explicit regularization and they are sufficiently decorrelated.
papers.limitation: Global features, such as gender and age, are harder to capture due to the patch-based prototypical encoder.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the opacity of diffusion-based generative models is urgently needed, as their applications continue to expand while their underlying procedures largely remain a black box. With a critical question -- how can the diffusion generation process be interpreted and understood? -- we proposed Patronus, an interpretable diffusion model that incorporates a prototypical network to encode semantics in visual patches, revealing what visual patterns are modeled and where and when they emerge throughout denoising. This interpretability of Patronus provides deeper insights into the generative mechanism, enabling the detection of shortcut learning via unwanted correlations and the tracing of semantic emergence across timesteps. We evaluate Patronus on four natural image datasets and one medical imaging dataset, demonstrating both faithful interpretability and strong generative performance. With this work, we open new avenues for understanding and steering diffusion models through prototype-based interpretability.\\ Our code is available at https://github.com/nina-weng/patronus}{https://github.com/nina-weng/patronus.

papers.title: Memorized Images in Diffusion Models share a Subspace that can be Located and Deleted
papers.research_question: Can memorization in diffusion models be localized to a specific subspace, and can pruning that subspace mitigate memorization without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization in diffusion models is localized to a compact subspace in the feed-forward layers, and pruning this subspace can mitigate memorization without retraining or interfering with inference.
papers.conclusion: Memorization in diffusion models can be localized to a compact subspace, and pruning this subspace is an effective, training-free method for mitigating memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in diffusion models is localized to a small set of neurons (a compact subspace) in the feed-forward layers.
Different sets of memorized prompts activate a common set of neurons, indicating a shared memorization subspace.
Pruning these neurons reduces memorization (as measured by SSCD) while maintaining image quality (CLIP score and FID).
The pruned models are robust to training data extraction attacks.
The method is computationally efficient and does not require modifications to the training or inference pipeline.
papers.limitation: The method requires a small set of memorized prompts as a starting point, while some inference-time mitigation techniques do not require memorized prompts.
papers.abstract: Large-scale text-to-image diffusion models excel in generating high-quality images from textual inputs, yet concerns arise as research indicates their tendency to memorize and replicate training data, raising We also addressed the issue of memorization in diffusion models, where models tend to replicate exact training samples raising copyright infringement and privacy issues. Efforts within the text-to-image community to address memorization explore causes such as data duplication, replicated captions, or trigger tokens, proposing per-prompt inference-time or training-time mitigation strategies. In this paper, we focus on the feed-forward layers and begin by contrasting neuron activations of a set of memorized and non-memorized prompts. Experiments reveal a surprising finding: many different sets of memorized prompts significantly activate a common subspace in the model, demonstrating, for the first time, that memorization in the diffusion models lies in a special subspace. Subsequently, we introduce a novel post-hoc method for editing pre-trained models, whereby memorization is mitigated through the straightforward pruning of weights in specialized subspaces, avoiding the need to disrupt the training or inference process as seen in prior research. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness of the pruned model against training data extraction attacks, thereby unveiling new avenues for a practical and one-for-all solution to memorization.

papers.title: The Hidden Language of Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the internal representations of textual concepts in text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CONCEPTOR, a method to decompose textual concepts in diffusion models into interpretable textual elements, revealing non-trivial structures in the learned representations such as visual connections, exemplar interpolations, and biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents CONCEPTOR, a method for interpreting concept representations in diffusion models, revealing non-trivial structures and biases, thus shedding light on the model's internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
CONCEPTOR decomposes concepts into a weighted combination of interpretable textual elements from the model's vocabulary.
It reveals visual connections between concepts that transcend their textual semantics (e.g., shape, texture, color).
Some concepts are represented as interpolations of exemplars (e.g., 'president' represented by famous presidents).
Homograph concepts can mix multiple meanings simultaneously in a single generated image.
CONCEPTOR can detect non-trivial social biases in concept representations that are not easily observable visually.
papers.limitation:
The visual impact of a decomposition element is not always completely aligned with its impact as a single token, as the effect depends on the context of the decomposition.
The method is limited to elements that are single tokens, so complex phrases cannot be included as a single element.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have demonstrated an unparalleled ability to generate high-quality, diverse images from a textual prompt. However, the internal representations learned by these models remain an enigma. In this work, we present Conceptor, a novel method to interpret the internal representation of a textual concept by a diffusion model. This interpretation is obtained by decomposing the concept into a small set of human-interpretable textual elements. Applied over the state-of-the-art Stable Diffusion model, Conceptor reveals non-trivial structures in the representations of concepts. For example, we find surprising visual connections between concepts, that transcend their textual semantics. We additionally discover concepts that rely on mixtures of exemplars, biases, renowned artistic styles, or a simultaneous fusion of multiple meanings of the concept. Through a large battery of experiments, we demonstrate Conceptor's ability to provide meaningful, robust, and faithful decompositions for a wide variety of abstract, concrete, and complex textual concepts, while allowing to naturally connect each decomposition element to its corresponding visual impact on the generated images. Our code will be available at: https://hila-chefer.github.io/Conceptor/

papers.title: Empirical Analysis of Decoding Biases in Masked Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: What are the decoding biases induced by uncertainty-based strategies in Masked Diffusion Models, and how can they be mitigated to improve generation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies rigid boundary bias and trivial token bias in uncertainty-based decoding for Masked Diffusion Models and proposes UNCODE, a decoding calibration framework that mitigates these biases, leading to improved performance on reasoning and planning tasks.
papers.conclusion: UNCODE effectively mitigates decoding biases in Masked Diffusion Models, enabling better reasoning trajectories and improved generation quality across diverse tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Rigid boundary bias causes MDMs to decode boundary tokens first, leading to premature answer resolution and suboptimal reasoning trajectories.
Trivial token bias prioritizes high-frequency, semantically trivial tokens, hindering the formation of critical reasoning steps.
UNCODE incorporates a positional trajectory prior to discourage rigid boundary-first decoding and a semantic informativeness prior to penalize trivial tokens.
UNCODE consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies by over 7% on average across seven benchmarks.
UNCODE enables MDMs to achieve performance comparable to autoregressive models of similar parameter scales.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs), which leverage bidirectional attention and a denoising process, are narrowing the performance gap with autoregressive models (ARMs). However, their internal attention mechanisms remain under-explored. This paper investigates the attention behaviors in MDMs, revealing the phenomenon of Attention Floating. Unlike ARMs, where attention converges to a fixed sink, MDMs exhibit dynamic, dispersed attention anchors that shift across denoising steps and layers. Further analysis reveals its Shallow Structure-Aware, Deep Content-Focused attention mechanism: shallow layers utilize floating tokens to build a global structural framework, while deeper layers allocate more capability toward capturing semantic content. Empirically, this distinctive attention pattern provides a mechanistic explanation for the strong in-context learning capabilities of MDMs, allowing them to double the performance compared to ARMs in knowledge-intensive tasks. All codes are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Uncode.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Finding NeMo: Localizing Neurons Responsible For Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we localize where memorization of individual data samples happens within diffusion models, down to the level of individual neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NEMO, the first method to localize memorization in diffusion models down to individual neurons, and shows that deactivating these neurons mitigates memorization without harming model performance.
papers.conclusion: NEMO successfully localizes memorization neurons in diffusion models, and deactivating them mitigates memorization while maintaining model performance, contributing to more responsible deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in diffusion models can be localized to individual neurons in the cross-attention layers, often just a single neuron.
Deactivating the identified memorization neurons prevents verbatim output of training data and increases diversity in generated images.
NEMO's approach is effective and comparable to existing inference-time mitigation strategies, but without requiring gradient computations or model retraining.
papers.limitation:
The search for memorization neurons is limited to value layers in the down- and mid-blocks of the U-Net, while other parts might also be involved.
The method requires a holdout dataset of non-memorized prompts to compute activation statistics for outlier detection.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) produce very detailed and high-quality images. Their power results from extensive training on large amounts of data, usually scraped from the internet without proper attribution or consent from content creators. Unfortunately, this practice raises privacy and intellectual property concerns, as DMs can memorize and later reproduce their potentially sensitive or copyrighted training images at inference time. Prior efforts prevent this issue by either changing the input to the diffusion process, thereby preventing the DM from generating memorized samples during inference, or removing the memorized data from training altogether. While those are viable solutions when the DM is developed and deployed in a secure and constantly monitored environment, they hold the risk of adversaries circumventing the safeguards and are not effective when the DM itself is publicly released. To solve the problem, we introduce NeMo, the first method to localize memorization of individual data samples down to the level of neurons in DMs' cross-attention layers. Through our experiments, we make the intriguing finding that in many cases, single neurons are responsible for memorizing particular training samples. By deactivating these memorization neurons, we can avoid the replication of training data at inference time, increase the diversity in the generated outputs, and mitigate the leakage of private and copyrighted data. In this way, our NeMo contributes to a more responsible deployment of DMs.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: Erasing Concepts from Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we erase undesirable visual concepts from pre-trained diffusion models using fine-tuning without additional data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a fine-tuning method called Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) that erases visual concepts from diffusion models using only concept descriptions and negative guidance, without additional data.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes an efficient method for erasing concepts from diffusion model weights, enabling safe distribution of parameters without the need for post-inference filters or expensive retraining.
papers.key_findings:
ESD effectively erases nudity content, performing on par with Safe Latent Diffusion and censored training.
ESD can remove artistic styles with minimal interference to other styles, as validated by a user study.
The method can erase entire object classes, though with some trade-off between erasure completeness and interference.
Fine-tuning cross-attention parameters allows for prompt-specific erasure, while non-cross-attention parameters enable global erasure.
The erasure strength η controls the trade-off between concept removal and image quality or interference.
papers.limitation:
Trade-off between complete erasure of a visual concept and interference with other concepts.
Incomplete erasure for some object classes, only removing distinctive attributes.
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent advancements in text-to-image diffusion, we study erasure of specific concepts from the model's weights. While Stable Diffusion has shown promise in producing explicit or realistic artwork, it has raised concerns regarding its potential for misuse. We propose a fine-tuning method that can erase a visual concept from a pre-trained diffusion model, given only the name of the style and using negative guidance as a teacher. We benchmark our method against previous approaches that remove sexually explicit content and demonstrate its effectiveness, performing on par with Safe Latent Diffusion and censored training. To evaluate artistic style removal, we conduct experiments erasing five modern artists from the network and conduct a user study to assess the human perception of the removed styles. Unlike previous methods, our approach can remove concepts from a diffusion model permanently rather than modifying the output at the inference time, so it cannot be circumvented even if a user has access to model weights. Our code, data, and results are available at https://erasing.baulab.info/

papers.title: DiffusionPID: Interpreting Diffusion via Partial Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How do individual tokens and their interactions in a text prompt shape the image generated by a text-to-image diffusion model? The paper investigates what diffusion models learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffusionPID, a method based on partial information decomposition (PID) to interpret text-to-image diffusion models by decomposing the input prompt into elementary components and analyzing uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy at both image and pixel levels.
papers.conclusion: DiffusionPID allows for a fine-grained understanding of the decision-making process in diffusion models, helping to identify shortcomings and reasons for failures. This understanding can be used to make diffusion models better aligned with human conceptual understanding and to counter their limitations and biases.
papers.key_findings:
DiffusionPID can reveal gender and ethnic biases in diffusion models by showing higher redundancy between stereotypical occupations and specific genders/ethnicities.
The method characterizes word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective, showing high synergy for homonyms with correct modifiers and high redundancy for synonyms.
DiffusionPID enables prompt intervention by identifying redundant words whose removal minimally affects the generated image.
The uniqueness maps can localize the most representative features of a concept, such as the bristles of a toothbrush.
The method provides fine-grained insights into model failures, such as confusing co-hyponyms due to high redundancy, leading to fused or missing objects in generations.
papers.limitation:
The method currently computes PID only for two phrases from the prompt, though it can be extended to more variables.
The approach requires access to the diffusion model, making it difficult to apply to closed-source models.
future_direction: Extending PID to more than two input variables.
Computing PID on other, non-diffusion-based models.
Exploring alternative methods of computing PID for closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have made significant progress in generating naturalistic images from textual inputs, and demonstrate the capacity to learn and represent complex visual-semantic relationships. While these diffusion models have achieved remarkable success, the underlying mechanisms driving their performance are not yet fully accounted for, with many unanswered questions surrounding what they learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize. Our work presents Diffusion Partial Information Decomposition (DiffusionPID), a novel technique that applies information-theoretic principles to decompose the input text prompt into its elementary components, enabling a detailed examination of how individual tokens and their interactions shape the generated image. We introduce a formal approach to analyze the uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy terms by applying PID to the denoising model at both the image and pixel level. This approach enables us to characterize how individual tokens and their interactions affect the model output. We first present a fine-grained analysis of characteristics utilized by the model to uniquely localize specific concepts, we then apply our approach in bias analysis and show it can recover gender and ethnicity biases. Finally, we use our method to visually characterize word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective and illustrate the efficacy of our method for prompt intervention. Our results show that PID is a potent tool for evaluating and diagnosing text-to-image diffusion models.

papers.title: Revealing the Attention Floating Mechanism in Masked Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: What is the attention mechanism in masked diffusion models (MDMs) and how does it differ from the attention sink phenomenon in autoregressive models (ARMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals the 'attention floating' phenomenon in masked diffusion models (MDMs), where dominant attention anchors shift dynamically across denoising steps and layers, and provides a mechanistic explanation for MDMs' superior in-context learning and robustness compared to autoregressive models (ARMs).
papers.conclusion: The attention floating phenomenon in MDMs provides a mechanistic explanation for their strong in-context learning and robustness, deepening the understanding of their internal workings.
papers.key_findings:
MDMs exhibit attention floating, where dominant attention anchors shift across denoising steps and layers, unlike the fixed attention sink in ARMs.
The attention mechanism in MDMs is shallow structure-aware and deep content-focused: shallow layers use floating tokens for global structure, deeper layers focus on semantic content.
MDMs show stronger in-context learning capabilities, nearly doubling performance gains of ARMs on knowledge-intensive tasks when using retrieved context.
MDMs are more robust to contextual noise, positional biases, and complex evidence layouts compared to ARMs.
Region-level attention flow analysis shows MDMs dynamically reorganize attention to track relevant context, while ARMs remain rigidly anchored at the sequence start.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses only on masked diffusion models (MDMs) and does not evaluate other diffusion language model variants.
The work is primarily mechanism analysis and does not propose training or inference methods to directly improve performance.
future_direction: Extend the analysis framework to a broader family of diffusion language models (DLLMs).
Propose training or inference methods that can directly improve performance based on the findings.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs), which leverage bidirectional attention and a denoising process, are narrowing the performance gap with autoregressive models (ARMs). However, their internal attention mechanisms remain under-explored. This paper investigates the attention behaviors in MDMs, revealing the phenomenon of Attention Floating. Unlike ARMs, where attention converges to a fixed sink, MDMs exhibit dynamic, dispersed attention anchors that shift across denoising steps and layers. Further analysis reveals its Shallow Structure-Aware, Deep Content-Focused attention mechanism: shallow layers utilize floating tokens to build a global structural framework, while deeper layers allocate more capability toward capturing semantic content. Empirically, this distinctive attention pattern provides a mechanistic explanation for the strong in-context learning capabilities of MDMs, allowing them to double the performance compared to ARMs in knowledge-intensive tasks. All codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Attention-Floating.

papers.title: CASL: Concept-Aligned Sparse Latents for Interpreting Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we align sparse latent dimensions of diffusion models with human-understandable semantic concepts to improve interpretability and control?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CASL, a supervised framework that aligns sparse latent dimensions of diffusion models with human-defined semantic concepts, enabling interpretable semantic control.
papers.conclusion: CASL provides a supervised framework for concept-aligned sparse latents, improving interpretability and control in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
CASL learns concept-aligned sparse latent directions that enable precise semantic editing with minimal unintended changes.
CASL-Steer, a controlled latent intervention, validates the semantic effect of aligned directions.
The proposed Editing Precision Ratio (EPR) metric effectively measures editing specificity and attribute preservation.
CASL outperforms existing methods in editing precision and interpretability.
The sparse autoencoder achieves good reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation: EPR metric is sensitive to the choice of attribute classifier and requires well-defined attribute labels, limiting its use in label-scarce or open-domain scenarios.
future_direction: Developing label-free editing precision metrics that remain valid across heterogeneous visual domains.
papers.abstract: Internal activations of diffusion models encode rich semantic information, but interpreting such representations remains challenging. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in disentangling latent representations, existing SAE-based methods for diffusion model understanding rely on unsupervised approaches that fail to align sparse features with human-understandable concepts. This limits their ability to provide reliable semantic control over generated images. We introduce CASL (Concept-Aligned Sparse Latents), a supervised framework that aligns sparse latent dimensions of diffusion models with semantic concepts. CASL first trains an SAE on frozen U-Net activations to obtain disentangled latent representations, and then learns a lightweight linear mapping that associates each concept with a small set of relevant latent dimensions. To validate the semantic meaning of these aligned directions, we propose CASL-Steer, a controlled latent intervention that shifts activations along the learned concept axis. Unlike editing methods, CASL-Steer is used solely as a causal probe to reveal how concept-aligned latents influence generated content. We further introduce the Editing Precision Ratio (EPR), a metric that jointly measures concept specificity and the preservation of unrelated attributes. Experiments show that our method achieves superior editing precision and interpretability compared to existing approaches. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to achieve supervised alignment between latent representations and semantic concepts in diffusion models.

papers.title: Unveiling and Mitigating Memorization in Text-to-image Diffusion Models through Cross Attention
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between memorization and cross-attention mechanisms in text-to-image diffusion models, and how can this be used to detect and mitigate memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that memorization in text-to-image diffusion models is associated with concentrated cross-attention on trigger tokens, and proposes efficient detection and mitigation methods based on attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a link between memorization and cross-attention concentration, and proposes effective detection and mitigation methods that preserve generation quality and speed.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization is characterized by concentrated cross-attention on trigger tokens, leading to higher attention entropy compared to non-memorization.
Different memorization types (matching, retrieval, template) exhibit distinct attention patterns on prompt and summary tokens.
The concentration of attention in memorization is more pronounced in specific U-Net layers, allowing early detection.
Inference-time mitigation via masking summary tokens and rescaling beginning token logits reduces memorization without compromising generation quality.
Training-time mitigation by filtering high-entropy samples effectively reduces memorization with minimal computational overhead.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-image diffusion models have demonstrated their remarkable capability to generate high-quality images from textual prompts. However, increasing research indicates that these models memorize and replicate images from their training data, raising tremendous concerns about potential copyright infringement and privacy risks. In our study, we provide a novel perspective to understand this memorization phenomenon by examining its relationship with cross-attention mechanisms. We reveal that during memorization, the cross-attention tends to focus disproportionately on the embeddings of specific tokens. The diffusion model is overfitted to these token embeddings, memorizing corresponding training images. To elucidate this phenomenon, we further identify and discuss various intrinsic findings of cross-attention that contribute to memorization. Building on these insights, we introduce an innovative approach to detect and mitigate memorization in diffusion models. The advantage of our proposed method is that it will not compromise the speed of either the training or the inference processes in these models while preserving the quality of generated images. Our code is available at https://github.com/renjie3/MemAttn .

papers.title: Unveiling Concept Attribution in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How do components in diffusion models contribute to a generated concept? How do model components work jointly to demonstrate knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CAD, a framework for attributing concept generation to model parameters in diffusion models, revealing both positive (concept-inducing) and negative (concept-suppressing) components, and introduces lightweight editing algorithms for concept erasure and amplification.
papers.conclusion: CAD provides a complete view of interpreting diffusion models by analyzing both positive and negative components, enabling better understanding and control of concept generation.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge is localized in a small number of parameters in diffusion models.
There exist negative components that suppress the generation of a target concept.
CAD-Erase effectively erases concepts by ablating positive components while preserving other knowledge.
CAD-Amplify amplifies concepts by ablating negative components, increasing the probability of generating the target concept.
CAD-based editing is robust against adversarial prompt attacks compared to other erasure methods.
papers.limitation:
Only focuses on model parameters, not other components like layers or modules.
Does not analyze attribution to specific stages in the reverse process or spatial locations in the image.
The proposed lightweight editing algorithms may not be the most performant; more sophisticated approaches (e.g., fine-tuning) could be developed.
Some components may be responsible for multiple concepts (entanglement), so ablating them can affect other knowledge.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other types of components (e.g., layers, modules).
Analyzing attribution to specific stages in the reverse process or spatial locations in the image.
Developing more sophisticated editing approaches, such as fine-tuning the influential components.
Studying the entanglement of parametric knowledge.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable abilities in generating realistic and high-quality images from text prompts. However, a trained model remains largely black-box; little do we know about the roles of its components in exhibiting a concept such as objects or styles. Recent works employ causal tracing to localize knowledge-storing layers in generative models without showing how other layers contribute to the target concept. In this work, we approach diffusion models' interpretability problem from a more general perspective and pose a question: \textit{``How do model components work jointly to demonstrate knowledge?''}. To answer this question, we decompose diffusion models using component attribution, systematically unveiling the importance of each component (specifically the model parameter) in generating a concept. The proposed framework, called \textbf{C}omponent \textbf{A}ttribution for \textbf{D}iffusion Model (CAD), discovers the localization of concept-inducing (positive) components, while interestingly uncovers another type of components that contribute negatively to generating a concept, which is missing in the previous knowledge localization work. Based on this holistic understanding of diffusion models, we introduce two fast, inference-time model editing algorithms, CAD-Erase and CAD-Amplify; in particular, CAD-Erase enables erasure and CAD-Amplify allows amplification of a generated concept by ablating the positive and negative components, respectively, while retaining knowledge of other concepts. Extensive experimental results validate the significance of both positive and negative components pinpointed by our framework, demonstrating the potential of providing a complete view of interpreting generative models. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/mail-research/CAD-attribution4diffusion}{here}.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
