The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Decoding Diffusion: A Scalable Framework for Unsupervised Analysis of Latent Space Biases and Representations Using Natural Language Prompts
papers.research_question: How to automatically map latent directions in diffusion models to semantic concepts using natural language prompts for scalable analysis of biases and representations?
papers.core_contribution: A framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion model latent spaces by mapping latent directions to natural language prompts, enabling automatic interpretation and broad concept analysis.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a scalable and versatile tool for interpreting diffusion model latent spaces, contributing to more transparent, interpretable, and ethically responsible generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework identifies gender biases in diffusion models, with professions like pilot and construction worker showing stronger male stereotypes.
Cosine distance between gendered and gender-neutral prompts correlates with the likelihood of generating female-presenting images.
Clustering of h-space vectors from food captions reveals semantic groups like square dishes and pots with soup.
The method enables automatic interpretation of latent directions without manual inspection.
It supports a broader range of analysis compared to previous methods limited by manual interpretation or few trained vectors.
papers.limitation: Variability due to random seed initialization affects the sampled h-space vectors.
future_direction: Reducing the effect of random seed initialization on sampled results
Extending analysis with quantifiable metrics on broader domains
papers.abstract: Recent advances in image generation have made diffusion models powerful tools for creating high-quality images. However, their iterative denoising process makes understanding and interpreting their semantic latent spaces more challenging than other generative models, such as GANs. Recent methods have attempted to address this issue by identifying semantically meaningful directions within the latent space. However, they often need manual interpretation or are limited in the number of vectors that can be trained, restricting their scope and utility. This paper proposes a novel framework for unsupervised exploration of diffusion latent spaces. We directly leverage natural language prompts and image captions to map latent directions. This method allows for the automatic understanding of hidden features and supports a broader range of analysis without the need to train specific vectors. Our method provides a more scalable and interpretable understanding of the semantic knowledge encoded within diffusion models, facilitating comprehensive analysis of latent biases and the nuanced representations these models learn. Experimental results show that our framework can uncover hidden patterns and associations in various domains, offering new insights into the interpretability of diffusion model latent spaces.

papers.title: SliderSpace: Decomposing the Visual Capabilities of Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can we automatically discover the visual structure within a diffusion model’s knowledge of a concept, enabling controllable and interpretable directions without manual specification?
papers.core_contribution: SliderSpace is a framework that automatically decomposes diffusion models' visual capabilities into semantically meaningful and controllable directions by performing spectral decomposition in semantic space and aligning low-rank adapters, enabling systematic exploration without manual attribute specification.
papers.conclusion: SliderSpace enables systematic exploration of diffusion models' latent creative space by automatically decomposing their capabilities into semantically meaningful and controllable directions without requiring manual attribute specification.
papers.key_findings:
SliderSpace decomposes high-level concepts into diverse and expressive components, revealing natural axes of variation in the model's understanding.
For artistic style exploration, SliderSpace discovers directions that match or exceed the diversity of manually curated artist lists and are judged more useful by human evaluators.
SliderSpace can reverse mode collapse in distilled diffusion models, restoring diversity while maintaining generation speed.
SliderSpace directions are transferable to related and out-of-domain concepts, indicating they capture fundamental visual transformations.
User studies show that SliderSpace-generated images are perceived as more diverse, useful, and creative compared to baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on semantic embeddings introduces biases present in the encoder's training data, which may not capture culturally-specific or nuanced artistic concepts.
The discovery process requires significant computational time (≈2 hours on an A100 GPU), limiting rapid experimentation.
Discovered art directions may not one-to-one match original artists.
future_direction: More careful study on choices of semantic embeddings and their effects on SliderSpace discovery.
Training time optimizations to reduce computational overhead.
Discovery that nudges directions to be aligned with real artists.
papers.abstract: We present SliderSpace, a framework for automatically decomposing the visual capabilities of diffusion models into controllable and human-understandable directions. Unlike existing control methods that require a user to specify attributes for each edit direction individually, SliderSpace discovers multiple interpretable and diverse directions simultaneously from a single text prompt. Each direction is trained as a low-rank adaptor, enabling compositional control and the discovery of surprising possibilities in the model's latent space. Through extensive experiments on state-of-the-art diffusion models, we demonstrate SliderSpace's effectiveness across three applications: concept decomposition, artistic style exploration, and diversity enhancement. Our quantitative evaluation shows that SliderSpace-discovered directions decompose the visual structure of model's knowledge effectively, offering insights into the latent capabilities encoded within diffusion models. User studies further validate that our method produces more diverse and useful variations compared to baselines. Our code, data and trained weights are available at https://sliderspace.baulab.info

papers.title: Not All Diffusion Model Activations Have Been Evaluated as Discriminative Features
papers.research_question: How to select a small yet effective subset of activations from diffusion models for discriminative tasks, given that many potential activations (e.g., within attention blocks and embedded ViT modules) have not been evaluated?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of diffusion U-Net activations, discovering three universal properties (asymmetric diffusion noises, in-resolution granularity changes, locality without positional embeddings) which enable qualitative filtering of sub-optimal activations, leading to an effective feature selection method that outperforms prior work on multiple discriminative tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed feature selection method, guided by the discovered universal properties of diffusion U-Nets, achieves state-of-the-art performance on semantic correspondence, semantic segmentation, and label-scarce segmentation tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Diffusion U-Nets exhibit asymmetric diffusion noises: activations in the early half of the up-stage are clean, while those in the down-stage and later up-stage are noisy.
In-resolution granularity changes are significant in modern 'fat' U-Nets, meaning activations within a single resolution can vary in information granularity.
ViT modules in diffusion U-Nets lack positional embeddings, leading to a weaker 'locality' property in self-attention activations where spatial proximity dominates over semantic similarity.
Locality in self-attention activations can suppress diffusion noises, making them preferable to severely noisy activations in high resolutions.
Feature selection solutions based on these properties, which include activations from ViT modules, outperform prior methods that only consider inter-module activations.
papers.limitation: The analysis and method are designed for U-Net based diffusion models and may not directly apply to other architectures like Diffusion Transformers (DiTs).
future_direction: Extend the analysis to Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models.
Explore the discovered properties in other types of generative models.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are initially designed for image generation. Recent research shows that the internal signals within their backbones, named activations, can also serve as dense features for various discriminative tasks such as semantic segmentation. Given numerous activations, selecting a small yet effective subset poses a fundamental problem. To this end, the early study of this field performs a large-scale quantitative comparison of the discriminative ability of the activations. However, we find that many potential activations have not been evaluated, such as the queries and keys used to compute attention scores. Moreover, recent advancements in diffusion architectures bring many new activations, such as those within embedded ViT modules. Both combined, activation selection remains unresolved but overlooked. To tackle this issue, this paper takes a further step with a much broader range of activations evaluated. Considering the significant increase in activations, a full-scale quantitative comparison is no longer operational. Instead, we seek to understand the properties of these activations, such that the activations that are clearly inferior can be filtered out in advance via simple qualitative evaluation. After careful analysis, we discover three properties universal among diffusion models, enabling this study to go beyond specific models. On top of this, we present effective feature selection solutions for several popular diffusion models. Finally, the experiments across multiple discriminative tasks validate the superiority of our method over the SOTA competitors. Our code is available at https://github.com/Darkbblue/generic-diffusion-feature.

papers.title: Canonical Latent Representations in Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify the underlying core categorical semantics in a conditional diffusion model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Canonical Latent Representations (CLAReps) in conditional diffusion models, which capture core class semantics with minimal irrelevant context, and a feature distillation paradigm (CaDistill) that uses CLAReps to improve student network robustness and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Conditional diffusion models can serve not only as image generators but also as compact, interpretable teachers that can drive robust representation learning through their canonical latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
CLARID identifies latent codes (CLAReps) whose internal CDM features preserve essential categorical information while discarding non-discriminative signals.
Decoded CLAReps produce Canonical Samples, which serve as interpretable and compact class prototypes.
The proposed feature distillation method, CaDistill, uses CLAReps to transfer core class knowledge, improving student adversarial robustness and generalization with only 10% of the training data size.
CLARID generalizes to different CDM architectures (e.g., DiT, Stable Diffusion) and diffusion samplers.
Feature clusters derived from CLAReps are more compact and separable than those from original samples, indicating better feature quality.
papers.limitation: CLARID can occasionally select suboptimal inversion time step (te) and number of extraneous directions (k), leading to artefacts in the generated Canonical Samples.
future_direction: Investigating how the semantic structure in text-conditioned models shapes the located CLAReps.
Exploring the use of pixel-space diffusion models on ImageNet for feature distillation.
Combining CaDistill with more sophisticated multi-layer feature distillation frameworks.
papers.abstract: Conditional diffusion models (CDMs) have shown impressive performance across a range of generative tasks. Their ability to model the full data distribution has opened new avenues for analysis-by-synthesis in downstream discriminative learning. However, this same modeling capacity causes CDMs to entangle the class-defining features with irrelevant context, posing challenges to extracting robust and interpretable representations. To this end, we identify Canonical LAtent Representations (CLAReps), latent codes whose internal CDM features preserve essential categorical information while discarding non-discriminative signals. When decoded, CLAReps produce representative samples for each class, offering an interpretable and compact summary of the core class semantics with minimal irrelevant details. Exploiting CLAReps, we develop a novel diffusion-based feature-distillation paradigm, CaDistill. While the student has full access to the training set, the CDM as teacher transfers core class knowledge only via CLAReps, which amounts to merely 10 % of the training data in size. After training, the student achieves strong adversarial robustness and generalization ability, focusing more on the class signals instead of spurious background cues. Our findings suggest that CDMs can serve not just as image generators but also as compact, interpretable teachers that can drive robust representation learning.

papers.title: Attention Sinks in Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of attention sinks in Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) and how do they differ from those in autoregressive models?
papers.core_contribution: DLMs exhibit dynamic attention sinks that shift during generation and are robust to masking, unlike autoregressive models, revealing fundamental differences in attention allocation.
papers.conclusion: DLMs have dynamic attention sinks and are robust to their removal, indicating flexible attention mechanisms that differ from autoregressive models.
papers.key_findings:
DLMs exhibit attention sinks, but they are dynamic and shift positions during the denoising process.
DLMs are robust to masking of attention sinks, with only minor performance degradation, unlike autoregressive models which are highly sensitive.
Different DLM architectures show distinct sink patterns: LLaDA-8B sinks are semantically based, Dream-7B sinks are positional, and MMaDA-8B sinks are static.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to instruct models and does not include base versions.
The study does not explore how modifications to the training procedure might influence sink behavior.
future_direction: Mechanistic analysis of what information is stored in sinks corresponding to future positions, e.g., using Logit Lens.
Exploring whether sinks could be exploited for acceleration or compression.
Detailed explanation of the observed sink phenomena, which would require an interpretability-focused study.
papers.abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to traditional Autoregressive Models (ARMs). DLMs employ transformer encoders with bidirectional attention, enabling parallel token generation while maintaining competitive performance. Although their efficiency and effectiveness have been extensively studied, the internal mechanisms that govern DLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis of DLM attention patterns, focusing on the attention sinking phenomenon, an effect previously observed in various transformer-based architectures. Our findings reveal that DLMs also exhibit attention sinks, but with distinct characteristics. First, unlike in ARMs, the sink positions in DLMs tend to shift throughout the generation process, displaying a dynamic behaviour. Second, while ARMs are highly sensitive to the removal of attention sinks, DLMs remain robust: masking sinks leads to only a minor degradation in performance. These results provide new insights into the inner workings of diffusion-based language models and highlight fundamental differences in how they allocate and utilize attention compared to autoregressive models.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/
